name: section
description: One band of a page. Eleven of them on the marketing site, spelled eight different ways — `px-5 py-12 sm:px-8 sm:py-14`, then `py-14 sm:py-16`, then `py-16 sm:py-20` — which is a vertical rhythm decided eight times rather than once. The gutter and the rule travel with it, because a section that sets its own padding and forgets its own divider is how a page loses its rhythm one edit at a time.
surfaceNote: every marketing band on every page

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

An explicit `display`, and it is load-bearing rather than tidy. `container-type: inline-size` has NO EFFECT on an element whose display is `inline` — containment needs a block box. This unit declared no display, so rendered as a `<span>` it was `inline`, its containment was inert, and every `@container` rule inside it silently never matched. The navbar found it: at 318px it was still showing a full desktop nav because the query it was waiting on could not fire.

The block padding is 1.6x the section step, not 1x. At 1x every band sat on the one above it with the same air between two sections as between two paragraphs inside one, so the page read as a single column of blocks rather than as a sequence of sections. Changed HERE rather than per page: it is the page's rhythm, and a rhythm set section by section is not one.

inner.$description: The measure. A section is full-bleed and its CONTENT is not — separating the two is what lets a band carry a colour to the edges while the text still stops at a readable width.

band.$description: A full-bleed band in the brand tone, carrying the one text colour a band has. The page's turning point, used sparingly — two on the home page.

primary.$description:
The MARINE band — the brand's own bar, and the page's strongest statement. It was missing from this vocabulary while being the ground of the home page's proposition band, so that section reached past the unit for a `bg-primary` utility: `band` is tidal and `band-alt` is a green-teal, and neither is the colour anyone meant. A ground the most important band on the site cannot name is a gap, not a preference.

IT RE-INKS WHAT IT HOSTS. Units carry the page's measured inks by design — `stat` sets `--color-foreground` on its figure and `--color-foreground-quiet` on its label — and inheritance never reaches a declared colour. So a ground that inverts owns re-inking its contents; the alternative is every unit growing a variant per ground. This is the same rule `navbar--tone-clear` follows for the language switch, and the same defect it was fixing.

The figure is `tertiary-edge`, not `turquoise`. The turquoise the band used measures 4.48:1 on marine and the figures are normal-size text needing 4.5 — short by two hundredths, which is exactly the kind of miss that survives review forever. `tertiary-edge` is the next step up the same hue at 5.62:1, so the figure stays turquoise and becomes legible.

measure.$description:
How wide the CONTENT runs inside a full-bleed section.

`wide` is 84rem, and 84rem is not a container on the screens people actually use: on a 1440px laptop it is 1344px — 93% of the viewport, with 48px of margin — which renders as edge-to-edge no matter that a max-width is technically applied. Measured, after the cap was reported broken and turned out to be working: the number was simply too large to read as one. `page` is the editorial measure for a section that has to feel held.

page.$description: 64rem. Wide enough for a two-column spread, narrow enough that the margins are visible on a laptop — which is what makes a page look composed rather than stretched. At 1440px this leaves ~200px either side; at 84rem it left 48.

a11y.note: A `<section>` is only a landmark when it has an accessible name, which is why `labelledBy` is on the interface rather than optional-by-habit. An unnamed section is a generic div to a screen reader, and a page of eleven of them gives a screen-reader user no way to skip between them.
